doc.title: Mike Longo interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 13, 2019

title: Becoming a Baha'i with Dizzy
summary: Longo describes his path to the Baha'i faith, Dizzy's near-death at the Village Vanguard, and Ray Brown's advice to keep asking Dizzy questions.

story.theme_name: Church, faith and religion in a musician's life
story.community_name: Church, faith and jazz: the sacred and the secular

blocks.x: Did his faith rub off on you?
No. The Baha’i faith itself rubbed off on me.

Dizzy became Baha’i five years before I did, but I had been studying it. I had an experience at the Jazz Workshop in Boston where I read it’s called the Long Healing Prayer. I awoke in the middle of the night in a panic man. I was like — anxiety. And I called this lady, Nancy Jordan, who was a Baha’i and her husband, Jordan, he was on the faculty at Yale or something, in the psychology department. She came to Boston and she had a pamphlet that talked about when you shed your old self and your real self comes out it feels like you’re dying. And so I calmed down and when I went to the gig that night I went to the piano and I played something on the piano and the piano said [hums]. I said man that’s the sound I’ve been looking for my whole life. I still hadn’t become a Baha’i yet. It took me — Dizzy almost died once at the Village Vanguard. I saved his life that night. Because somebody gave him a drug that he thought was one thing and it turned out to be something else. And so I said, “Man if you’ll let Dizzy pull through I’ll be a Baha’i you know. We were out of work for six weeks. And so the next gig was at the Playboy Club in St. Louis. And that club was in a hotel and so our rooms were right upstairs. And so man something told me to ask Dizzy at the rehearsal I said, “Man, can you show me that thing you do on the drum, that African thing?” And the lady that had talked Dizzy into being a Baha’i happened to be there. And she gave me the card to sign. And I’m looking at these bunnies saying do I really want to do this? And so I became a Baha’i and that night after Dizzy showed me that, I got on the bandstand and Dizzy said, “God damn, what did you do man?” And from that point on, because I remember I was playing — Redd Foxx had a club in L.A. And so Ray Brown came to the gig to hear us. And Ray had been at the school with Oscar when I studied there. So he said, “Man, Dizzy’s not going to teach you cats like he did us in the 40s,” he said, “but ask him questions. Keep asking him questions.” So I spent the next twenty years asking him every kind of question. And so that’s how I learned all that stuff, from him.
